series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 1/1] mm/swap: allocate contiguous swap slots for a reclaim batch
series_items.patch_summary: This patch optimizes swap slot allocation by allocating contiguous slots in batches, reducing the number of small write requests and improving performance. It achieves this by recording the number of pages of each order that need a slot before swapping out a batch, and then making those allocations follow contiguous free slots. This approach helps to minimize the fragmentation of swap clusters and reduces the overhead of small write requests.

review_comments.author: Nhat Pham
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer Nhat Pham expressed concerns that the patch does not address workloads that benefit more from disk swapping than compression swapping, and requested further consideration for these use cases.

Reviewer noted that the patch does not apply its contiguous allocation heuristic to folios larger than a certain order, and found this omission reasonable.

Reviewer Nhat Pham expressed concern that the patch's preference for non-full clusters with contiguous slots may lead to increased lock contention, especially as swapfiles become more fragmented.

Reviewer Nhat Pham raised concerns about the effectiveness of the contiguous swap slot allocation heuristic, questioning whether it would lead to overshooting the estimate and creating problems down the line. They also suggested that this heuristic might not be necessary for cgroups that enable zswap or zram.
review_comments.raw_body:
Thanks for looking into this! There are still workloads that benefit
more from disk swapping than compression swapping... We should make
the swap subsystem work for them.

I haven't read the code too closely, as it's an RFC meant to show the
general idea. So I'll just make some comments and ask some questions
about the idea:

---

Ah so we don't invoke this heuristics for folio larger than certain
orders? Makes sense.

---

So we prefer non-full clusters with contiguous slots, over free
clusters, over other nonfull clusters.

I think this part makes sense to me FWIW. We do skip fast path and go
for slow paths more often, so do make sure we're not paying with too
much lock contention, especially as the swapfile fils or get more
fragmented (which this patch series does nudge us towards). But FWIW,
we pretty much go back to the old behavior the moment we fail to find
contiguity for the first time in the batch, so I think we'll be
fine...?

---

Some general questions:

1. How many pages in folio_list typically do get reclaimed? There can
be quite a few with references, which we rotate/promote, when we scan,
right? Would constantly overshooting the estimate create problem down
the line?

(This is one of the few places where indirection (vswap) would have
helped - we can collect a batch of pages after unmapping, then pass
them to the phys swap allocator (after checking zswappability, etc.).
Maybe we can solve it better after it's landed, and accept an
imperfect solution for now?)

2. Should we skip this heuristics for cgroups that enables zswap (and
maybe zram)? Contiguity matters less there... unless it help at
writeback time? Hard to say without experimentation - maybe you can do
the same check you did for your zswap writeback batching patch series?

review_comments.author: Alexandre Ghiti
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer noted that the folio_alloc_swap_split() function is not properly handling the case where a batch of LRU-adjacent folios spans multiple free clusters, and requested that the function be modified to allocate contiguous swap slots for such cases.

Reviewer Alexandre Ghiti noted that large folios have a separate allocation scheme and suggested adding this detail to the changelog.

Reviewer Alexandre Ghiti expressed a neutral sentiment by stating they would investigate the impact of this patch on zswap and writeback, but did not provide any specific technical concerns or suggestions.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch aims to reduce the number of I/O requests on a swap device by keeping reclaim batches contiguous. The current implementation of swap allocation and deallocation can lead to scattered writes, resulting in increased I/O requests. The patch modifies the allocator to allocate contiguous free slots for a reclaim batch, reducing the number of small requests and improving throughput. This is achieved by informing the allocator about the size of the batch and allowing it to allocate contiguous slots accordingly. The goal is to reduce the overhead of swap I/O operations and improve system performance.

review_comments.summary: Reviewer Kairui Song suggested reverting commit 9a42aed48421, which prefers nonfull over free clusters for small order allocations, and instead always scanning full clusters to prioritize contiguity on large physical swap devices.
review_comments.raw_body:
Hi Alexandre,

That's a interesting problem. I think the real problem is with commit
9a42aed48421 ("mm, swap: prefer nonfull over free clusters"), right?

It's more like a balance between fragmentation and contiguity of small
order allocation issue.

Perhaps we should instead always scan the full clusters and revert
that one commit? That commit was only following the idea of keeping
the allocation more compacted for that series, it looked good at that
time. Since fragmentation issues can be solved in other ways,
contiguity seems to matter more for large physical swap devices.

I encountered this myself. Remember when I wrote my own swap allocator
for vswap? In one of the version, I went for free clusters first
instead of partial clusters. It fragmented the swap space, so I had to
copy your homework and went for partially used clusters first...

Anyway, maybe I'm wrong - some numbers would be nice here.

review_comments.summary:
Reviewer suggested limiting the patch's scope to SYNC devices or exploring simpler solutions to address the problem, expressing skepticism about the significance of a 4% reduction in mTHP failures.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 01/12] mm/page_alloc: reset can_retry_reserves when the slowpath restarts
series_items.patch_summary: This patch series aims to improve the page allocation mechanism in the Linux kernel by resetting a flag called can_retry_reserves when the slowpath restarts after certain events, such as cpuset updates or zonelist rebuilds. The goal is to ensure that memory allocations are retried correctly even in the presence of these events.

review_comments.author: Zi Yan
review_comments.summary: Approved the patch with a positive sentiment, indicating that it is ready for merge.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Sat Oct 31, 2026 at 10:13 PM EDT, Gregory Price (Meta) wrote:
> Commit 2c4c3e29897d ("mm/page_alloc: simplify __alloc_pages_slowpath()
> flow") retries an allocation once with reserve_flags when the caller
> becomes eligible for reserves, guarded by can_retry_reserves.
>
> A restart after a cpuset update or a zonelist rebuild retries with
> can_retry_reserves already set to false, so a caller that cannot
> reclaim (GFP_NOWAIT | __GFP_MEMALLOC), fails without trying reserves.
>
> Reset can_retry_reserves on restart. Only a cpuset or zonelist change
> restarts the slowpath, so the retry still runs at most once per change.
>
> With a kprobe helping to make the race deterministic, an allocation
> can be made to return NULL. With this patch the allocation will succeed.
>
> Fixes: 2c4c3e29897d ("mm/page_alloc: simplify __alloc_pages_slowpath() flow")

series_items.patch_summary: This patch prevents the pagesets of an empty zone from being freed prematurely, which can cause corruption when a new owner takes over the per-cpu memory. Instead, it keeps the existing pagesets and allows setup_zone_pageset() to reuse them. This fix addresses a problem introduced by a previous commit that freed the pagesets when a zone became empty.

series_items.patch_summary: This patch series aims to improve the accuracy of oom detection tracepoints by passing the zone pointer instead of the zoneref pointer in the reclaim_retry_zone tracepoint. This change is necessary because memory hotplug rebuilds the zonelists in place while allocations are under way, which can lead to incorrect zone identification.

review_comments.summary: Identified the problem with zonelist rebuilds and agreed that passing the zone pointer is a good solution.

> to the reclaim_retry_zone tracepoint, which loads the zone from the

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 04/12] mm/page_alloc: detect zonelist rebuilds from memory hot-add
series_items.patch_summary: This patch series addresses a memory hot-add issue in the Linux kernel's page allocation mechanism. Specifically, it detects zonelist rebuilds from memory hot-add and fixes a race condition between build_all_zonelists and page allocation. The fix involves gating sequence checks on CONFIG_MEMORY_HOTPLUG to cover all configurations that rebuild zonelists after boot.

review_comments.author: Zi Yan
review_comments.summary: Acknowledged the patch with Acked-by, indicating they are satisfied with its technical quality and content.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Sat Oct 31, 2026 at 10:13 PM EDT, Gregory Price (Meta) wrote:
> The zonelist_update_seq retry was limited to CONFIG_MEMORY_HOTREMOVE,
> presumably because only hot-remove takes zones out of a zonelist.
>
> However, build_zonerefs_node() rewrites the zonelists in place, so
> onlining the first block of a zone shifts the entries that follow it
> in every zonelist containing that zone.  This can cause a spurious
> allocation failure for a __GFP_THISNODE caller.
>
> For a node with only ZONE_NORMAL, onlining its first ZONE_MOVABLE block
> rewrites the node's ZONELIST_NOFALLBACK list as:
>
>   [NORMAL, NULL] -> [MOVABLE, NULL] -> [MOVABLE, NORMAL, NULL]
>
> A concurrent GFP_KERNEL | __GFP_THISNODE allocation can observe the
> intermediate list, skip ZONE_MOVABLE, and find no eligible zone. With
> CONFIG_MEMORY_HOTREMOVE=n, check_retry_zonelist() returns 0 and the
> allocation fails even though the node has free ZONE_NORMAL memory.
>
> Gate the sequence checks on CONFIG_MEMORY_HOTPLUG, which covers every
> configuration that rebuilds zonelists after boot.
>
> Fixes: 3d36424b3b58 ("mm/page_alloc: fix race condition between build_all_zonelists and page allocation")
> Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
> Reviewed-by: Vlastimil Babka (SUSE) <vbabka@kernel.org>

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 05/12] mm/mmzone: read the zoneref slot once in zonelist_zone()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch addresses a memory hotplug issue where zonelists are rebuilt in place, causing the zoneref slot to change between loads. It uses READ_ONCE() to ensure that the zone is loaded only once.

review_comments.author: Zi Yan
review_comments.summary: Identified the issue and approved the fix, suggesting that READ_ONCE() is sufficient to prevent the zoneref slot from changing between loads.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Sat Oct 31, 2026 at 10:13 PM EDT, Gregory Price (Meta) wrote:
> Memory hotplug rebuilds zonelists in place while allocations walk them,
> so a zoneref slot can change between two loads of it.
>
> zonelist_zone() loads the slot with a plain access.  The compiler may
> load it again later instead of keeping the zone it already read, so a
> caller can check one zone and then use another, or the NULL terminator.
>
> Use READ_ONCE().  Callers that take a zone from a slot and keep using
> it, such as get_page_from_freelist() with ac->preferred_zoneref, need
> that single load.
>
> Fixes: 11cd8638c37f ("mm, page_alloc: remove stop_machine from build_all_zonelists")

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 06/12] mm/page_alloc: snapshot the preferred zone against shrink rebuilds
series_items.patch_summary: This patch addresses a kernel NULL pointer dereference bug in the page allocation code by introducing a snapshot of the preferred zone against concurrent zonelist rebuilds. The preferred zone is read only once, and if it becomes stale or NULL due to concurrent rebuilds, the function fails as expected. This fix removes the need for repeated reads of the preferred zone, which can lead to bugs like the one reported.

This change fixes an issue where kprobes holding the walk across the online could cause a fault to take a page from the wrong node.

The zonelist_update_seq retry was limited to CONFIG_MEMORY_HOTREMOVE,
presumably because only hot-remove takes zones out of a zonelist.

However, build_zonerefs_node() rewrites the zonelists in place, so
onlining the first block of a zone shifts the entries that follow it
in every zonelist containing that zone.  This can cause a spurious
allocation failure for a __GFP_THISNODE caller.

For a node with only ZONE_NORMAL, onlining its first ZONE_MOVABLE block
rewrites the node's ZONELIST_NOFALLBACK list as:

  [NORMAL, NULL] -> [MOVABLE, NULL] -> [MOVABLE, NORMAL, NULL]

intermediate list, skip ZONE_MOVABLE, and find no eligible zone. With
CONFIG_MEMORY_HOTREMOVE=n, check_retry_zonelist() returns 0 and the
allocation fails even though the node has free ZONE_NORMAL memory.

configuration that rebuilds zonelists after boot.

zone->per_cpu_pageset and zone->per_cpu_zonestats. Nothing waits for those
who found the zone populated and still use the two pointers. They take
neither the memory hotplug lock nor any other lock which offline_pages()
holds, and some of them can sleep:

    for_each_populated_zone(zone)

      cond_resched()
                                      adjust_present_page_count()
                                      zone_pcp_reset(zone)
                                        free_percpu(zone->per_cpu_pageset)
      decay_pcp_high(zone, pcp)
      __this_cpu_write(pcp->expire, 0)

zone_pcp_update(), show_free_areas() and the readers and writers of the
zonestats. If the per-cpu memory has got a new owner in the meantime, it
is corrupted.

leak them when the zone gets memory again. Keep them instead and let
setup_zone_pageset() and zone_pcp_init() use them again, like it is done

have been calculated for a zone without memory by the
init_per_zone_wmark_min() of offline_pages(), which is what
setup_zone_pageset() would come up with as well.

Memory hotplug rebuilds zonelists in place while allocations walk them,
so a zoneref slot can change between two loads of it.

zonelist_zone() loads the slot with a plain access.  The compiler may
load it again later instead of keeping the zone it already read, so a
caller can check one zone and then use another, or the NULL terminator.

Use READ_ONCE().  Callers that take a zone from a slot and keep using
it, such as get_page_from_freelist() with ac->preferred_zoneref, need
that single load.

@@ -1855,7 +1855,8 @@ extern struct zone *next_zone(struct zone *zone);

 {
-	return zoneref->zone;
+	/* Memory hotplug rewrites zonelists in place. */
+	return READ_ONCE(zoneref->zone);
 }

__next_zones_zonelist() tests a slot's zone for NULL, then reads the
slot again to look up the zone's node. Offlining a zone's last block
rebuilds the zonelists in place, so the second read can return the
terminator:

  CPU 0                             CPU 1
  __next_zones_zonelist(nodemask)
    zonelist_zone(slot 1) = NORMAL
                                    offline_pages()
                                      build_all_zonelists()
                                        [MOVABLE, NORMAL, NULL]
                                        -> [NORMAL, NULL]
    zref_in_nodemask(slot 1)
      zone_to_nid(NULL)

Current GCC and clang merge the two reads, but nothing requires it.
With mm/mmzone.o built with -fno-inline -fno-ipa-sra, holding a
nodemask allocation between the reads while the node's last movable
block goes offline oopses every time:

  RIP: 0010:zone_to_nid+0x0/0x10
  Call Trace:
   zref_in_nodemask+0x9/0x20
   __next_zones_zonelist+0x23/0x70
   prepare_alloc_pages.constprop.0+0x16c/0x190
   __alloc_frozen_pages_noprof+0xaf/0x330

Onlining the first block of a zone rebuilds every zonelist in place,
shifting the slots after the new zone.  The iterator approves a slot,
then the allocator loads the zone from it, so a GFP_KERNEL request can
land in ZONE_MOVABLE and a nodemask request on a node outside its mask:

  CPU 0                             CPU 1
  prepare_alloc_pages()
    first_zones_zonelist(nodemask {1})
      slot 0 (NORMAL1) approved
                                    online_pages()
                                      build_all_zonelists()
                                        [NORMAL1, NORMAL2, ...]
                                        -> [MOVABLE1, NORMAL1, ...]
  get_page_from_freelist()
    zone = zonelist_zone(slot 0)    /* MOVABLE1 */
    allocates from MOVABLE1

zonelist_update_seq detects the rebuild, but only the slowpath's failure
exits check it.

Check it whenever an allocation succeeds too, and if it changed, free
the page and retry, as the memcg charge failure path does.  Eligible
pages are dropped as well: zonelists only change when memory comes or
goes, and a retry is simpler than rechecking the page.

Freeing the page does not undo a block the allocation claimed.  A
GFP_KERNEL request that lands in a fresh ZONE_MOVABLE converts a free
block to MIGRATE_UNMOVABLE, which stays until the zone's movable free
list runs out and a movable allocation takes it back.

The fast and bulk paths read the seqlock's raw seqcount without waiting:
an ALLOC_NOLOCK caller can be an NMI that interrupted the writer, and on
PREEMPT_RT the seqlock accessor takes the spinlock.  A sample taken
mid-write costs a retry, or NULL under ALLOC_NOLOCK.
check_retry_zonelist() returns 0 when compiled out, so a backport
without the hot-add change stays harmless.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 1/4] mm/huge_memory: scale thp_underused() to the folio size
series_items.patch_summary: This patch updates the thp_underused() function to be aware of the size of a folio, rather than just PMD-sized folios. It scales the khugepaged_max_ptes_none threshold proportionally to the number of pages in the folio, ensuring that the same fraction of zero-filled pages is tolerated for any folio size. This change will prevent issues when collapsing mTHP orders and splitting folios, as both operations would use the same threshold for a given folio size. The patch makes no functional changes for PMD-sized folios, as their page count is always HPAGE_PMD_NR.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 2/4] mm/huge_memory: don't queue folios when underused splitting is inactive
series_items.patch_summary: This patch optimizes the handling of anonymous PMD-sized folios in huge memory by skipping their queueing when underused splitting is inactive, which is the default configuration. This change is motivated by the fact that at the default sysctl maximum, no folio is ever underused and thus there's no need to queue them for splitting. The patch also factors out this check into a new function `thp_underused_never()` to share it between two functions.

On 03/11/2026 21:20, Joanne Koong wrote:
> Every anonymous PMD-sized folio is put on the deferred split queue when
> it is first mapped, so that the shrinker can find it under memory
> pressure and split it if it turns out to be mostly zero-filled.
> 
> With the default khugepaged/max_ptes_none this is wasted work. The
> default is HPAGE_PMD_NR - 1, which tells thp_underused() that any number
> of zero-filled pages is tolerable, which means the shrinker will never
> split any of these folios for being underused. They take the list_lru
> lock at fault time, inflate the object count the shrinker reports, and
> are then walked and dropped when they're first scanned.

> factor that check out into thp_underused_never() so that
> deferred_split_folio() and thp_underused() share it. Since the default
> is the maximum, out of the box no folio is queued for underused

> paying for that on every anonymous fault.

> queued before khugepaged/max_ptes_none is lowered gets dropped from the

On Wed, Nov 4, 2026 at 5:20 AM Joanne Koong <joannelkoong@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Unlike for PMD-sized folios, an anonymous mTHP folio doesn't get added
> to the deferred split list at fault or collapse time. As a result, a
> fully mapped mTHP folio that is mostly zero-filled doesn't get split by
> the deferred split shrinker when the system is under memory pressure.
>
> At Meta we would like to deploy 2M THP=always on arm64 with 64k base
> pages, as 2M gives the contpte benefits while the PMD size (512M) is too
> big to use. Without underused splitting this causes memory regressions,
> as the unused parts of those folios can never be broken down and
> reclaimed.
>
> Add anonymous mTHP folios to the deferred split list from
> map_anon_folio_pte_nopf(), mirroring what map_anon_folio_pmd_nopf()
> already does for PMD-sized folios. This covers both the fault path and
> the khugepaged mTHP collapse path. If there is memory pressure, a
> zero-filled mTHP can then be split with its zero pages remapped to the
> shared zero page and reclaimed.

> thp_underused() scaling khugepaged/max_ptes_none to the folio size, any

>
> To minimize overhead on the common order-0 fault path, the

>

series_items.subject: [PATCH v8 2/7] mm/page_counter: introduce per-CPU stock
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a per-CPU stock representation in the page_counter layer, similar to memcg's seven-slot per-CPU stock. It adds a new struct page_counter_stock_pcp that preserves the existing behavior from memcg and includes a backpointer to the base of the percpu stock. The patch also updates the page_counter structure to include pointers to the percpu stock and its owning cgroup_subsys_state. No functional changes are intended in this patch, which is part of a larger series.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v8 3/7] mm/page_counter: make page_counter_try_charge() stock-aware
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the page_counter_try_charge function to be aware of stock, allowing it to consume stock transparently while preserving existing semantics. Two new parameters are added: may_batch and nr_charged. The first parameter preserves the behavior in !allow_spinning scenarios, where charges are made as quickly as possible without evicting other stock slots. The second parameter reflects the size of a successful hierarchy charge, used for memory.high accounting heuristics.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v8 4/7] mm/memcontrol: check PF_MEMALLOC after trying the limits
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the behavior of memory charging in Linux to check for PF_MEMALLOC after trying limits, rather than before. This change is necessary because a later patch moves the memory stock into the page counter, leaving no room between consuming the stock and trying limits for the PF_MEMALLOC check. The patch checks for PF_MEMALLOC on both outcomes of the page counter charge, skipping memory.high on success and forcing the charge on failure.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v8 5/7] mm/memcontrol: move memory stock to page counters
series_items.patch_summary: This patch moves the memory stock from memcg to page counters, allowing for more efficient and accurate memory management. The change preserves the legacy user-visible relationship between memory and swap usage, even when their raw values temporarily diverge. It also introduces a new logic to prevent reclaiming swap space when both memory and swap have equal limits. The patch removes unused code from memcg and prepares it for future work on introducing additional page counters without breaking the fast path.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v8 6/7] mm/memcontrol: add stock to the memsw page counter
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a separate stock to the memsw page counter, allowing it to operate independently of the memory bank. The common drain scheduling is factored into schedule_stock_drain(), which handles both stocks uniformly. If memory charge fails, only the nr_pages from memsw are rolled back. This change enables the raw counters for memory and memsw to temporarily drift due to cached amounts, while preserving the user-visible cgroup-v1 invariant.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v8 7/7] mm/memcontrol: restrict memory stock to leaf cgroups on v2
series_items.patch_summary: This patch restricts memory stock to leaf cgroups in the new page_counter_stock world, ensuring that stock does not get stranded in the hierarchy and cannot be used by processes that actually charge. It achieves this by preventing stock from accumulating in non-leaf page_counters through three methods: clearing the parent's memory stock pointer, scheduling drains for non-isolated CPUs, and lazily cleaning up CPUs that are not drained due to isolation or racing with a refill. The patch also re-enables stock when a parent becomes a leaf again.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series moves the stock implementation from memcontrol to page_counter, allowing for better separation of charge caching and policy management. The stock is a per-CPU cache of precharged pages that speeds up small allocations by avoiding frequent walks of the page_counter hierarchy. By moving it to page_counter, the patch simplifies the handling of stock in non-leaf cgroups and prepares for future improvements. It also ensures that locking behavior remains unchanged and that exact charging is preserved for non-spinning callers.

series_items.patch_summary: This patch series addresses a critical issue in the arm64 SDEI (System Description Event Infrastructure) implementation, where an SDEI event dispatched from user space can cause the CPU to loop indefinitely due to zero-filled trampoline vectors. The fix involves installing kernel vectors when VBAR_EL1 holds the trampoline vectors and restoring them before returning to firmware.

patches_submitted.subject: [RFC PATCH v2 00/18] mm: read the page cache without folio references

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v2 01/18] mm: free PG_rcu_free folios only after an RCU grace period
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a new page flag, PG_rcu_free, which allows folios to be freed only after an RCU (Read-Copy Update) grace period. This is done to prevent CPUs from bouncing the refcount of a file being read, and to allow readers to access the folio until the RCU grace period has passed. The patch adds support for this flag in various kernel components, including page flags, vmstat, and memory failure handling. It also introduces a new workqueue to handle freeing deferred pages during an RCU grace period.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v2 02/18] splice: don't steal page cache folios
series_items.patch_summary: This RFC patch series proposes to remove the ability for splice operations to steal page cache folios, which can lead to premature folio refcount drops and potential data corruption. The change involves dropping the ->try_steal function from page_cache_pipe_buf_ops and modifying fuse_try_move_folio() and virtio_console's pipe_to_sg() to copy instead of stealing when SPLICE_F_MOVE is set.

review_comments.author: David Hildenbrand
review_comments.summary: Identified potential performance implications of removing page cache folio stealing, including temporary increased memory consumption and potential slowdowns for certain workloads. Requested additional context on why the change is necessary.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v2 03/18] fuse: don't move a folio with PG_rcu_free into a fuse file
series_items.patch_summary: This patch prevents a folio marked for RCU freeing from being moved into a fuse file, which can lead to issues when the folio is still being copied by a lockless page cache read. This happens in specific scenarios where a mapped file page is gifted and then truncated. The patch instead copies such a folio as fuse would do if it cannot take one. This change ensures that fuse files handle folios marked for RCU freeing correctly.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v2 04/18] mm: count the pages waiting for a grace period
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new counter, NR_FREE_RCU_PAGES, to track pages waiting for an RCU (Read-Copy Update) grace period. These pages have refcount 0 and are not on the free lists, making them invisible to existing counters. The patch updates several functions in the mm module to include this new counter in various statistics, such as /proc/vmstat and show_free_areas(). This change is a preparation step for freeing these waiting pages sooner when they hold back needed memory.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v2 05/18] mm: expedite the grace period when a CPU has many deferred frees
series_items.patch_summary: This patch aims to improve the performance of deferred frees in the Linux kernel by introducing an expedited grace period when a CPU has many pending folios (memory allocations). When more than 4 MiB is pending on a CPU, the patch takes both lists and frees them after an expedited grace period. This approach ensures that memory is freed quickly when it's needed, without waiting for the normal grace period. The patch also introduces a new counter in /proc/vmstat to track the number of times this expedited process has freed memory. The goal is to prevent memory bottlenecks and improve system responsiveness, especially during bulk frees triggered by operations like file truncation or fadvise(POSIX_FADV_DONTNEED).

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v2 06/18] mm: free the pages waiting for a grace period before OOM
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the Linux kernel's memory management to free pages waiting for a grace period before invoking the Out-Of-Memory (OOM) killer. When reclaim fails, it checks if freeing these waiting pages and what reclaim can still free would bring an eligible zone above its minimum watermark. If so, it drains these pages straight to the buddy lists, allowing the OOM killer to be invoked only when necessary. This approach is designed to reduce the likelihood of invoking the OOM killer unnecessarily, which can lead to system instability.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v2 07/18] mm: free the pages waiting for a grace period before isolation fails
series_items.patch_summary: This patch addresses an issue where migration of pages to a new zone fails due to pages waiting for a grace period after being freed. The patch introduces a new function, `rcu_free_sync()`, which frees all waiting folios and their associated work. This allows the allocation process to proceed without failing due to pending page migrations. The change is made in two key functions: `offline_pages()` and `alloc_contig_range()`. In `offline_pages()`, if a migration pass has occurred and there are pages waiting for a grace period, the function calls `rcu_free_sync()` before retrying the allocation. Similarly, in `alloc_contig_range()`, if the check for isolated pages fails due to pending migrations, the function frees any waiting folios before attempting to allocate memory again.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v2 08/18] mm/compaction: free the migrated folios that wait for a grace period
series_items.patch_summary: This patch addresses an issue in the Linux kernel's compaction mechanism, where migrated folios that wait for a grace period can cause compaction to fail more often. The problem arises when a block is migrated and its folios are not immediately freed, causing subsequent migrations to occur unnecessarily. To resolve this, the patch introduces a new function `rcu_free_drain()` that frees these waiting folios before draining the per-cpu lists. This change improves compaction efficiency and reduces allocation stalls in defrag_mode.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v2 09/18] mm/memory-failure: handle folios with PG_rcu_free
series_items.patch_summary: This patch addresses an issue where memory_failure() and soft_offline_page() cannot handle pages that are waiting for an RCU (Read-Copy-Update) grace period, which causes them to be ignored or handled incorrectly. The patch introduces a new function mf_free_rcu_pages() that frees these pages before attempting to access them, ensuring they are properly handled by memory_failure(). Additionally, it modifies the get_any_page() and memory_failure() functions to wait for an RCU grace period after setting PG_hwpoison on a page, allowing readers to safely unmap the poisoned page. This patch aims to improve the handling of pages waiting for an RCU grace period in the Linux kernel's memory failure mechanism.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v2 10/18] mm: have folio_mark_accessed() return whether the folio is hot
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the `folio_mark_accessed` function to return a boolean value indicating whether the accessed folio is considered 'hot'. A hot folio is one that is either unevictable or has its access flags set. This change prepares for reading the status of folios without requiring an explicit reference to them. The patch updates the `folio_mark_accessed` function and related code in the Linux kernel's memory management (mm) module.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v2 11/18] mm/filemap: mark a folio accessed in one place in filemap_read()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch simplifies the filemap_read() function by moving the folio access marking into a single helper function, filemap_read_accessed(). This function is called once per folio in the loop, eliminating duplicate code and making it easier to decide which folios are worth reading without a reference. The change does not affect the behavior of the function, but prepares for future improvements.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v2 12/18] mm/filemap: set PG_rcu_free on the folios that reads keep coming back to
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a new flag, PG_rcu_free, which allows the kernel to delay freeing memory associated with a folio that is frequently accessed by readers. The flag is set in filemap_read() when a folio is found to be hot based on LRU records or previous read access patterns. This approach aims to balance the trade-off between delaying free of streaming reads and truncating files, while also avoiding unnecessary delays for cold data. The patch includes changes to various kernel files to support this new flag and provide statistics on its usage.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v2 13/18] mm/filemap: read from the page cache without folio references
series_items.patch_summary: This patch improves the page cache read performance by allowing reads to occur without taking a reference on the folio, reducing the bounce of refcounts between CPUs. It achieves this by copying data from folios that are about to be freed under RCU read lock and using a batch size of up to 512 KiB per section. The patch also optimizes large folios and introduces checks for poisoned pages, uptodate status, and other conditions that require the slow path. This approach aims to reduce overhead and improve performance in scenarios with multiple CPUs accessing the same file.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v2 14/18] mm/filemap: read large folios without folio references
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the Linux kernel's filemap module to allow reading large folios without creating a reference to them. A large folio is one that spans all or none of its range, and once the last page in its range is reached, subsequent pages can be copied from the same folio. The patch introduces a new function `filemap_read_rcu_size` to calculate how much data can be copied from a folio without creating a reference. It also updates the `filemap_read_rcu_lookup` function to handle large folios and split them correctly when necessary. This change aims to improve performance by reducing the number of references created during file I/O operations.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v2 15/18] mm/filemap: don't store f_ra.prev_pos for FMODE_RANDOM files
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the filemap_read function to skip storing f_ra.prev_pos for files that have FMODE_RANDOM set, which is used by applications like RocksDB to read files at random offsets from multiple threads. The patch addresses a performance issue where reads were slower due to unnecessary shared store operations. It keeps the slow path of the function intact and only skips the store operation when filemap_read_rcu has already done a full read without folio references.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v2 16/18] mm/shmem: count accesses to a folio the way filemap_read() does
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the way accesses to a folio in tmpfs are counted. Instead of only marking a folio as accessed when a read starts at its beginning, it marks the folio accessed unless the previous read through the file ended in the same position. This change ensures that reads that start anywhere within a folio count towards its access age, rather than just those that start at the beginning. Additionally, this patch sets PG_rcu_free on tmpfs folios that are repeatedly accessed.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v2 17/18] mm/shmem: read without folio references
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the shmem_file_read_iter function to take a reference on every folio it reads, which can cause small reads of one tmpfs file from many CPUs to bounce the folio's refcount. To fix this issue, the patch introduces a new function called filemap_read_rcu that copies data from the page cache without taking any references. This function is used in place of shmem_file_read_iter for small reads, allowing multiple CPUs to read from the same tmpfs file simultaneously without causing reference count bounces.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v2 18/18] mm/filemap: add a debugfs switch for lockless page cache reads
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a debugfs switch to control lockless page cache reads in the Linux kernel. The goal is to provide a way to turn off lockless reads, which can be problematic for certain workloads or when there's a bug in the read path. The switch is added as a static key that can be enabled or disabled through debugfs. When enabled, it stops filemap_read() and shmem_file_read_iter() from setting PG_rcu_free and copying without a reference. This allows users to test and verify the correctness of lockless reads before they are enabled by default.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series proposes a change to how Linux handles page cache reads, allowing multiple CPUs to read from the same folio without taking a reference. This is done by introducing a new flag PG_rcu_free and deferring the freeing of folios until an RCU grace period. The goal is to reduce contention between readers and improve performance in scenarios where many threads are reading the same pages. The patch series includes 18 patches that implement this change, including modifications to filemap_read(), shmem, and other related functions.

From: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Reading a page cache folio without taking a reference would keep CPUs
that read the same file from bouncing its refcount.  But without a
reference the folio can be freed, and its memory reused, while the
reader copies from it.

Add PG_rcu_free: the free of a folio with the flag waits for an RCU
grace period.  A reader that saw the flag under rcu_read_lock(), and
then still found the folio where it looked, can read it until
rcu_read_unlock().  A split copies the flag, as such a reader may still
be reading the new folios.

The folios wait on per-CPU lists, one grace period in flight per CPU:
call_rcu() per folio would queue a callback for every folio of a
truncated file.  A work, which can reschedule, frees each batch.
Reclaim depends on these frees, so the workqueue is WQ_MEM_RECLAIM.

The flag is 64-bit only (CONFIG_PAGE_RCU_FREE): page flags are scarce
on 32-bit, and the contention this avoids is a problem of large
machines.  It is off on PREEMPT_RT, where expedited grace periods are
normal ones, so the waiting pages cannot be freed quickly when memory
runs short.

pgfree_rcu in /proc/vmstat counts the deferred pages.  Nothing sets the
flag yet.

+
+static struct workqueue_struct *rcu_free_wq __ro_after_init;
+
+static void rcu_free_start(struct rcu_free_pcpu *r)
+{
+	lockdep_assert_held(&r->lock);
+
+	if (r->queued || list_empty(&r->pending))
+		return;
+
+	list_splice_init(&r->pending, &r->batch);
+	r->queued = true;
+	WARN_ON_ONCE(!queue_rcu_work(rcu_free_wq, &r->rwork));
+}
+
+static void rcu_free_pages(struct list_head *list)
+{
+	struct folio_batch fbatch;
+	struct folio *folio, *next;
+
+	folio_batch_init(&fbatch);
+	list_for_each_entry_safe(folio, next, list, lru) {
+		if (!folio_batch_add(&fbatch, folio)) {
+			free_unref_folios(&fbatch);
+			cond_resched_tasks_rcu_qs();
+		}
+	}
+	if (folio_batch_count(&fbatch))
+		free_unref_folios(&fbatch);
+}
+
+static void rcu_free_workfn(struct work_struct *work)
+{
+	struct rcu_free_pcpu *r = container_of(to_rcu_work(work),
+					       struct rcu_free_pcpu, rwork);
+	LIST_HEAD(done);
+
+	spin_lock_irq(&r->lock);
+	list_splice_init(&r->batch, &done);
+	r->queued = false;
+	rcu_free_start(r);
+	spin_unlock_irq(&r->lock);
+
+	rcu_free_pages(&done);
+}
+
+static void rcu_free_defer(struct folio *folio)
+{
+	struct rcu_free_pcpu *r = raw_cpu_ptr(&rcu_free_pcpu);
+	unsigned long flags;
+
+	spin_lock_irqsave(&r->lock, flags);
+	list_add_tail(&folio->lru, &r->pending);
+	rcu_free_start(r);
+	spin_unlock_irqrestore(&r->lock, flags);
+}
+
+static void __init rcu_free_init(void)
+{
+	int cpu;
+
+	if (!IS_ENABLED(CONFIG_PAGE_RCU_FREE))
+		return;
+
+	rcu_free_wq = alloc_workqueue("rcu_free",
+				      WQ_MEM_RECLAIM | WQ_PERCPU, 0);
+
+	for_each_possible_cpu(cpu) {
+		struct rcu_free_pcpu *r = per_cpu_ptr(&rcu_free_pcpu, cpu);
+
+		spin_lock_init(&r->lock);
+		INIT_LIST_HEAD(&r->pending);
+		INIT_LIST_HEAD(&r->batch);
+		INIT_RCU_WORK(&r->rwork, rcu_free_workfn);
+	}

review_comments.summary: The author is addressing a concern about the reuse of page cache folios in fuse and virtio consoles, specifically that stolen pipe buffers are reused without being freed. The author agrees to remove the ->try_steal function from page_cache_pipe_buf_ops, which will prevent this issue.
review_comments.raw_body:
From: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

PG_rcu_free holds back the reuse of a folio's memory until a grace
period after the folio is freed.  A stolen page cache pipe buffer is
reused without being freed: remove_mapping() takes the folio out of the
page cache and the caller keeps it.  fuse_try_move_folio() puts it into
a fuse file, where writes change it under a reader that found it before
the steal.

Drop ->try_steal from page_cache_pipe_buf_ops.  fuse_try_move_folio()
and virtio_console's pipe_to_sg() then copy, as they already do when
stealing fails.  SPLICE_F_MOVE from the page cache into a fuse file or
a virtio console now copies.

Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
[kas: rewrote the changelog]
Signed-off-by: Kiryl Shutsemau (Meta) <kas@kernel.org>

@@ -55,56 +55,6 @@ static noinline void pipe_clear_nowait(struct file *file)
 	} while (!try_cmpxchg(&file->f_mode, &fmode, fmode & ~FMODE_NOWAIT));
 }
 
-/*
- * Attempt to steal a page from a pipe buffer. This should perhaps go into
- * a vm helper function, it's already simplified quite a bit by the
- * addition of remove_mapping(). If success is returned, the caller may
- * attempt to reuse this page for another destination.
- */
-static bool page_cache_pipe_buf_try_steal(struct pipe_inode_info *pipe,
-		struct pipe_buffer *buf)
-{
-	struct folio *folio = page_folio(buf->page);
-	struct address_space *mapping;
-
-	folio_lock(folio);
-
-	mapping = folio_mapping(folio);
-	if (mapping) {
-		WARN_ON(!folio_test_uptodate(folio));

-		/*
-		 * At least for ext2 with nobh option, we need to wait on

-		}
-	}

fuse_try_move_folio() takes the folio of a pipe buffer and puts it into
a fuse file, where writes change it.  A folio with PG_rcu_free may still

review_comments.author: Kiryl (Meta) (author)
review_comments.summary: The author addressed a concern about the interaction between memory hotplug and RCU free pages, explaining that alloc_contig_range() and offline_pages() migrate folios out of a range but then check if every page is free, which fails when a migrated folio has PG_rcu_free. The author proposed to free waiting folios before checking, allowing alloc_contig_range() to find the start of the free range again.

review_comments.author: Kiryl (Meta) (author)
review_comments.summary: The author addressed the concern that compaction fails more often when migrating blocks containing PG_rcu_free folios, which are freed after a grace period. The author agreed to restructure the code in v2 to free pages waiting for a grace period before draining per-cpu lists and checking if compaction is done.
review_comments.raw_body:
A block that compaction has migrated every folio out of becomes free
once those folios are back in the buddy lists.  A migrated folio that
had PG_rcu_free comes back only after a grace period, so compaction
finds the block still in use, migrates more blocks than it needs and
fails more often.  defrag_mode relies on compaction making whole free
blocks, and there it shows up as allocation stalls.

When compaction moves past a block it migrated from and the zone has
pages waiting, free them before it drains the per-cpu lists and checks
whether it is done.  The drain costs an expedited grace period, so
async compaction, which must not block, skips it.

+				 * Folios migrated away from lockless readers
+				 * are freed after a grace period.  Async
+				 * compaction does not wait for it.

+					rcu_free_drain();

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH] crash: keep crashkernel CMA pages reserved if activation fails

version_history.subject: [PATCH] crash: keep crashkernel CMA pages reserved if activation fails

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch modifies the crashkernel memory reservation mechanism to keep CMA pages reserved even if their activation fails. This ensures that kernel data written to these pages is not overwritten by the crash kernel and remains available in the dump. The change adds a new function call, cma_reserve_pages_on_error(), which marks the areas as reserved when activation fails.

review_comments.author: Bradley Morgan
review_comments.summary: The reviewer noted that the patch's behavior of marking crashkernel CMA areas as reserved on activation error would also occur under every bitmap_zalloc() failure, and asked if this is accounted for.
review_comments.raw_body:
You do know that this will activate under every bitmap_zalloc() failure,
right? Is that accounted for?

review_comments.author: Usama Arif (author)
review_comments.summary: The author addressed Bradley Morgan's concern about the crashkernel CMA pages being released when activation fails, explaining that keeping them reserved ensures the first kernel doesn't overwrite or lose data from the vmcore. The author confirmed this is the intended behavior and mentioned an alternative approach in fadump.
review_comments.raw_body:
Yes, that's intended. By the time cma_activate_area() runs, the range is
already in crashk_cma_ranges[], so the crash kernel will use it no matter
why activation failed. Keeping the pages reserved is the only way to make
sure the first kernel has nothing there that gets overwritten or goes
missing from the vmcore; the area then behaves like a regular
crashkernel= reservation of the same size.

fadump made the same choice; it is what cma_reserve_pages_on_error() was
added for in commit 27d121d0ec6d ("mm/cma: provide option to opt out
from exposing pages on activation failure").

The bitmap is one bit per page (32 KiB per GiB with 4K pages) and is
allocated at core_initcall, so a failure there is very unlikely.

The alternative is to give the memory back and to drop the
range from crashk_cma_ranges[] when activation fails, leaving the crash
kernel with less memory than requested. I do think that is acceptable as
well. But we do need either whats done in this patch or give the memory
back. Happy to send the alternative as v2 is everyone thinks that the
better way forward.

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH] mm/hugetlb: allow crashkernel to reuse hugetlb CMA memory

version_history.subject: [PATCH] mm/hugetlb: allow crashkernel to reuse hugetlb CMA memory

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch allows the crashkernel to reuse existing hugetlb CMA memory, enabling systems that already reserve large amounts of memory with hugetlb_cma= to use some of it for the capture kernel's working set after a crash. The patch introduces a new suffix 'hugetlb_cma' for the crashkernel parameter, which allows specifying an additional amount of memory to be reused from existing HugeTLB allocations. This approach ensures that the running kernel can still access the full 6G of hugetlb CMA memory during normal operation, while providing the capture kernel with additional working memory after a crash.

review_comments.author: Kiryl Shutsemau
review_comments.summary: Reviewer noted that the new suffix in crashkernel=size,hugetlb_cma does not provide any additional information beyond what is already stated in the documentation for crashkernel=size,cma. They suggested reusing existing hugetlb CMA memory first and reserving a dedicated area only for what hugetlb CMA does not cover.
review_comments.raw_body:
The crashkernel=size,cma documentation already says that pages allocated
from the range are not in the vmcore and that it should not be used if
dumping of userspace memory is intended. HugeTLB pages are userspace
memory. I don't see what a new suffix makes explicit that ",cma" does
not already.

Why not let crashkernel=size,cma take hugetlb CMA first and reserve a
dedicated area only for what hugetlb CMA does not cover? With
hugetlb_cma=6G crashkernel=2G,cma there would be no extra CMA at all.
With hugetlb_cma=2G crashkernel=4G,cma the crash kernel would reuse the
2G and a dedicated 2G area would be reserved for the rest. Either way,
nobody has to learn a new option.

The catch is ordering. reserve_crashkernel_cma() runs from setup_arch(),
but hugetlb_cma_reserve() runs later, from mm_core_init_early(). The arch
code could record the size and leave the reservation to generic code
right after hugetlb_cma_reserve(). That is still memblock time, so the
remainder can be declared there. An early_initcall is too late for that.

-- 
  Kiryl Shutsemau / Kirill A. Shutemov
